utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please be seated. Mr. Registrar, would you please have the accused brought in? I would like to see if all the interpreters can hear me. Very good. I hope you've been able to take advantage of this morning as we all have. The Office of the Prosecutor hears me. And the accused hears me, the Defence. I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see we're ready to resume. Before we bring in the witness, I don't want to be mistaken about his name. I believe his name is Dusan Bilandzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, do you hear me? Very well. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination has not been completed. Therefore, I give, without further ado, the floor to Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, in your testimony yesterday in response to some questions by my learned colleague, Mr. Nobilo, you noted that every nation, and I apologise, I'm dealing from page 11.288, counsel, line 14: "Every nation passes through this phase. It is a phase of nationalism which turns into chauvinism and leads to war. Every nation is to apply another principle in addition to the ethnic principle, at least one, and that is the principle of historic right." "I have the right, as a leader of a nation, to establish borders along those countries who, at some time in history, say, a thousand years ago, were within the composition of my one-time ruler." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think, and correct me if I'm wrong at any point in this series of questions, Doctor, in conjunction with that you highlighted for the Court the studies by the, I believe, 19th Century linguist, and again, if I'm wrong on the "19th Century", please correct me, but the 19th Century linguist Vuk Karadzic, who noted that because people in the Balkans or certain areas of the Balkans, I believe you noted from Salonika to Constantinople, spoke essentially the same language, they were one nation, and when asked what nation he noted that nation was a Serb nation. I think you testified that that, in conjunction with some other factors, fuelled the belief for a Greater Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That is partially correct, but partly, I think, you misunderstood, as you misunderstood the interpretation of the first two principles, that is the ethnic principle, and the historic right to a national state, which I think has been quite totally misinterpreted but I shall explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The ethnic principle is -- has been more or less accepted in our civilisation. It was advocated by the American president, President Wilson, and the Russian leader Lenin, the right of nations to self-determination on the basis of their ethnic or national affiliation. As for the principle of rights based on history, the historic right to lands that used to belong to someone in the past, this was never accepted, nor did I interpret that principle as being a correct one, but this was advocated by those who had the idea of creating greater national states outside the ethnic right. So that is not my position, nor has that been accepted as something generally applicable in modern civilisation. Which doesn't mean to say that wars are not waged in the name of that principle. They have been waged in the past and they are being waged today. As for the second point, our time is limited for me to explain this, but these are shades of meaning in defining the ethnos from the Austrian border to the Black Sea, Salonika and so on. This was a period when the ideology of Panslavism was prevalent, as well as the ideology of Yugoslavism, so that theoreticians for certain political aims and for certain other reasons, added to this the following thesis, that these were still not sufficiently crystallised or sufficiently developed national consciousness, that these were peoples who had still not differentiated among themselves, who are mixed together using the same or a similar language, but advantage of the Serb language was that it could become that pillar which assisted by the political actions of the state, and, of course, by other means, would speed up the process in support of this main nucleus, which, according to Karadzic, and to Tucic (Phoen) was Serbia itself. So there are various shades of meaning to that theory, and because of the limitation of time I had to simplify some of these theoretical premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Doctor, but you do reject the thesis of Karadzic, that for instance, Croats, living in the Balkans are all Serbs? You reject that argument of Vuk Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, during your time as a historian and as a politician, you are familiar, and again we are talking on the discussion, the point you brought out yesterday on a possible interpretation of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and during your time as a historian and as a politician, you were familiar with the writings of President Tudjman, and I believe in the article that we have before you, and if it's not it can be placed before the witness, Exhibit 464, you noted in this Nacional article that, "Tudjman never published a single article without letting me read it first." So you were intimately familiar with his ideas; were you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I will give you the floor, but first I would like to know, is this a Prosecution exhibit, the document we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is an exhibit we saw yesterday. 464 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is trying to cross-examine the witness about scholarly and other works by President Tudjman. However, the subject of the examination-in-chief was not the life of President Tudjman but the break-up of Yugoslavia. And President Tudjman, just before the break up of Yugoslavia, took over the lead in Croatia, and in that period he had not written anything. So he was not a relevant factor until he became the leader of Croatia. He was not relevant in the life of the former Yugoslavia. So this is a cross-examination beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a very free journalist interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One moment, please. Let's make sure we maintain some order. I'm not sure if I understood the question -- first of all I would like to hear the question put by the Prosecutor on this matter and then I will turn to my colleagues. It seems that the witness wishes to respond to the question, but I have retained the observation you have made, Mr. Nobilo. Now, very quickly, will you please tell me the sense of you question and after that I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The sense of my question and the cross-examination is this, Mr. President: The witness has offered us an explanation for the decline and fall of the former Yugoslavia, laying the fault, in large part, on President Milosevic of Serbia. In part, if you recall the testimony yesterday, one of the five things or five powerful items that the witness testified that Milosevic used, was the nationalistic fervour that Milosevic, for lack after better word, drummed up in Serbia and elsewhere for the Greater Serbia movement. He noted at the outset of his discussions, Mr. President, that this was one possible interpretation. I am attempting to cross-examine this particular witness on a parallel similar, dissecting cause for the decline and fall of the former Yugoslavia. Case in point, we talked yesterday about the meetings in Karadjordjevo where quite clearly this witness in a newspaper article on the 25th of October 1993...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Let me now consult with my colleagues. Thank you, my colleagues. Your objection is overruled, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Kehoe you may continue with your questioning and the line that you have just clarified. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, as a historian and as a politician, you are familiar with some of President Tudjman's writings, especially on the national question, are you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: May I make a remark? Regarding the interpretations of history. The historical sciences take the position that it is not possible to give a definitive interpretation of history. Hundreds of monographs have been devoted to Napoleon, for instance, and each author pretends to be correct. I have spoken to students and saying I wish we had ten different textbooks, historical textbooks about the history of the Croatian people or any other people, because it is never possible to say that only one interpretation is valid. A British historian, whose name I cannot recall, has written a book entitled "The History of the Habsburg Monarchy." I have read it and I could write an anti-history. Therefore, in history as a science, there is no final definitive truth. History is always open to various interpretations, and that is my position as a scholar, and that is why I said that this is one possible interpretation, and that others will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, I --

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I can understand you because you are not a historian and you need not know that history opens up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Professor, it's a legal discussion, this is not a historic conference. I understand you have a great number of things to say, but we need to cut back to the subject at hand. The Prosecutor has put a question to you, I'll ask that the Prosecutor put a question to you and you respond to that question. I understand what you mean by historical interpretations, but I would like for Mr. Kehoe to put his question briefly to you, and that he do so immediately, and then that he receive a response from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, I appreciate that the British historians that wrote the history of the Habsburgs, being it Crankshaw, be it McQuiggan or be it Wheatcroft, which I believe are all British?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do not go back to the old British monarchy issue, please. Ask your question with regards to the issue at hand, otherwise we will never be able to get out of the issue about a historical conference. Please ask your question with regards to the article Nacional, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: None of those first historians became the President of the Republic Croatia, did they?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't understand the meaning of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please ask the question that you now wish to ask. The British monarchy is not really our favourite question, but of course, if you're interested in that subject please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: President Tudjman wrote a book called "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe". You're familiar with that book, are you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I have not held that book in my hands. I did read the book the war against war, and the book on the creation of socialist Yugoslavia, and occupation during the second world war, because it is not correct, I have to caution you. As a rule, do I not authorise interviews that I give to the press. I leave that up to the consciousness of the journalists -- the conscience of the journalists. And journalists, as you know, that is their profession, tend sometimes to exaggerate things, to overemphasise, to leave out other things, so it is not true that I have read everything that Tudjman has written, or rather, that he didn't publish anything before I read it that is a complete invention. I repeat, I do not authorise my interviews, and all the journalists in Zagreb know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we put Exhibit 16 back on the ELMO, please? For counsel's ease of purposes for the next line of questions, we'll be talking about Exhibit 19. Exhibit 19, for Your Honours' clarification, is Franjo Tudjman's book, "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe." Now, Doctor, I will read you a portion of this, beginning on the top of page 113. And in this discussion, Doctor, the author, Dr. Franjo Tudjman is discussing the decision to unite Vojvodina with Serbia, and he notes, after analysing some factors: "According to the same yardstick, Bosnia-Herzegovina should have been made part of the Croatian Federal Unit. Bosnia-Herzegovina were historically linked with Croatia, and together they comprise an indivisible geographic and economic entity. Bosnia-Herzegovina occupy the central part of this whole separating southern Dalmatian from northern Panonian Croatia. The creation after separate Bosnia-Herzegovina makes the territorial and geographic position of Croatia extremely unnatural in the economic sense, and, therefore, in the broadest national political sense very unfavourable for life and development." Now, we turn to the map that's before you. "These factors largely explain why the 1939 agreement between Belgrade and Zagreb included the following areas of Bosnia into the banovina of Croatia. The whole of western Herzegovina and Mostar, and those of Bosnia districts where the Croats have a clear majority, Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bugonjno, Fojnica, Travnik, Derventa, Karadzic and Brcko. On the next page and I will not read the entire page, but starting from the first full paragraph, counsel. "An objective examination of the numerical composition of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot ignore that the majority of the Muslims in its ethnic character and speech" -- excuse me, "the majority of Muslims is, in its ethnic character and speech, incontrovertibly of Croatian origin. Despite religious and cultural distinctions created by history, the vast majority of the Muslims declared themselves Croats whenever an opportunity arose." And we move, counsel, for the sake of reading, to the bottom of the page, the last two sentences. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with -- counsel is reading from Exhibit 18. But what has been provided to him is a map of the Vance-Owen Plan, which is Exhibit. So the witness doesn't have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right. The last two sentences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When and the judges have nothing at all. Nor do the interpreters, so although you have read slowly, what is on the ELMO at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is a map of the bonavina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see we have the map before us. As for the rest of the objection from Mr. Hayman --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel meant to put this book passage before the witness, I think. What was provided to him is a map of the Vance-Owen Plan, which is Exhibit 19, so the witness isn't able to follow the quotations that counsel is reading. I simply ask that Exhibit 18, which is the book except, be provided to the witness so that he can have the benefit of being able to see the printed text, although it is not in his native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I can do, Mr. President, is do that, read it slowly as it's being interpreted. The matter on the ELMO is the bonavina plan, it is not a map of anything else other than the bonavina plan and that's what's being discussed in this article by President Tudjman. So I have two sentences left to read, Mr. President, and we will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go on then, but please read slowly so that the witness can follow. And the contents of the passage of President Tudjman. I'm sorry, one moment. Professor, would you like for us to have this passage reread slowly in your language so that you understand fully the question which will be placed to you there after? Would you like for us to have this reread? I'm referring to the passage from Mr. Tudjman's book.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My learned colleague was correct. This is Exhibit 18, my personal records were incorrect. I apologise in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The final sentence I will read to you, and I will not read any further, and after citing various facts, Dr. Tudjman writes that on the basis of these facts, we arrive at the conclusion that a majority of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina is Croatian. Now, Doctor, did President Tudjman ever tell you that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No. But if you would like to hear my interpretation of the quotation from President Tudjman's book, I must tell you, unfortunately, that I have not read that text, and even if I had read it, it would require a certain amount of time to prepare for a scientific analysis of this text which cannot be made ad hoc, because such text require such an approach. And secondly, in historiography in Yugoslavia, both in Serb history and Croatian history, there is the thesis that the Muslims are a Slav people who, at a certain point in time, converted to Islam. According to the Serb version, these were Serbs who converted to Islam, and a certain section of Croatian authors, in fact it was the dominant theory in the 19th Century that they were Croats. So this is a generally known fact in history. This is nothing new. But I wouldn't like to elaborate on this issue, because in that case we would have to apply the standards of historical science.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, when you went to Tikves in April of 1991, you knew that President Tudjman's position --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise to my learned colleague, but we had an objection yesterday, and the court sustained it, that questions related to Tikves and Karadjordjevo have been covered repeatedly and been dealt with. So we're going back to what the court ruled out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are, with all due respect, there are numerous questions -- not numerous, but several very important issues concerning this very important secret meeting in Karadjordjevo that need to be asked of this witness. Keeping in mind that this is not a historian who simply wrote or thought about this issue, this is a historian who was sent to a meeting by President Tudjman to discuss secretly with other Serbs issues concerning the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Chamber has the following opinion: First of all, the rule with regard to the cross-examination. That rule has been established to ensure the proper conduct of these proceedings. At the same time, you must show some flexibility at times because this is not a mechanical rule; rather it is a rule of common sense and left to the discretion of the judges. That is the second observation. The third observation in this same are, Mr. Nobilio, is that the judges and this Chamber feels that it is their duty, when it is necessary, to request as the rules of procedure allows them to do so, that we go to the very depth of any particular issue, so that we can exhaust any aspect of any particular question. This thing the judges feel that the issue of Karavo Istasin (Phoen), even though you do not see the importance that should be attached to this. Nonetheless, on this particular principle alone we determine that Mr. Kehoe will be permitted to ask questions about this place of meeting. It is the judges who solemnly believe that we must, whenever possible, ascertain the truth and therefore we will allow the question to be put to the professor on this issue. Therefore, Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you knew in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Pardon, on this issue, perhaps I might conclude by stating and reassuring the Defence that you do indeed have the right for a rejoinder following this cross-examination. Please go on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you knew in 1991 that in Croatia, there was a group of politicians that advocated the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be incorporated into the Republic of Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That is an assumption which you are taking as being absolutely correct. Croatian policy, at that time, held very firmly, adhered firmly to one stand and that is that the borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia according to the constitution are state borders and Croatia does not accept any change in the borders. As far as other matters are concerned, as a confrontation was expected, there could have been some steps taken about which I have absolutely no proof either written or oral and what I said I remain adamant. I think that I elaborated it yesterday and I really have nothing to add to this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you gave an interview to the -- on the tape that we heard, dispatches where you said the truth about the Karadjordjevo meeting was never officially published. They were secret talks, but the impression was given to the media and that the talks were only about the disputes between Croatia and Serbia, nothing else. Did you not say that on the tape, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't know if they were secret and they were secret, not only those, but the practice was introduced after the regime was changed in Yugoslavia that all, practically all the meetings, I think all meetings, in fact, were secret meetings. So if they're secret, then I don't know what they could have discussed there because I have no documents on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, if you want, I will run the tape back for you because it's very brief. But did you say in an interview on camera that we reviewed yesterday that these were secret talks and that the truth about those meetings had not been revealed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. If you wish to have the tape played, then, please, we can have it played and that will be very short and very simple. Judge Riad would also like to have this tape replayed. I don't know about Judge Shahabuddeen, but we can do so. The judges do wish for this to be done. So let us play this tape once again and that way the professor will be able to hear his on words and be able to say whether or not he stands by them. Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there seems to be a misunderstanding. The professor has confirmed that they were secret and that he has no information about that. He keeps repeating that. Despite that fact, my learned colleague is raising new questions as to what happened there. What is there on the tape is what he says to stay there. It was a secret meeting and I have no information on those talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a fundamental difference this time because this time it is the judges that are requesting that the tape be replayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Gentlemen in the video booth, it's the first clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kehoe, please be very direct, very concise with the very concrete question you wish to put in the course of your cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, I go back to my initial question. These were secret talks between the Serbs and the Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Every man on the street will tell you that if the mass media did not publish a communiqué and documents from some talks, every citizen will tell you if you ask him what the talks were and what kind of talks they were. They will say they were secret talks because they were not publicly disclosed, so they cannot be classified or qualified in any other way. You can't qualify a meeting, you have to say that it was a secret meeting. I see no other logical explanation. That is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Both the Serb government and the Croatian government misled the media on the purpose of those meetings in Karadjordjevo, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: As far I remember, neither the Croatian nor the Serbian government, they didn't explain anything to the mass media, I don't know where that source comes from, that they published anything. I don't remember the source. I have no source in my possession that any explanation was given of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But President Tudjman, Doctor, told you about the secret, didn't he? He told you that he had made a deal with Milosevic about the division of Bosnia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Not quite in that way. You asked me whether those two governments, the Serbian and the Croatian explained to the public. That was the question about the meeting. And I said that I don't know, I didn't know. Tudjman didn't tell me that he had decided on -- but that he wanted to see the relationships between those two states. And I repeat what I have already said five times. The expert group had an academic discussion over the question of whether to recognise the borders of the existing republics and then left because the Serbian delegation, they parted then, because the Serbian delegation considered that these were not state borders and we considered that they were state borders and that is all that I have to say about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I turn your attention, again, Doctor, Exhibit 464, the newspaper article that we discussed yesterday, because I think that I need to clarify some points from the statement that you just made. Is that article before the witness? If we can turn again to the second page in the lower left-hand column, Doctor. Do you need your glasses, Doctor? We can wait. Please. Just a moment. Mr. President, the witness needs his eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see well enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you sure, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree with my colleague, it's difficult to read. If we want to take a moment to wait for his glasses, it might be a little more expeditious all the way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's one's fundamental rights to be able to read with one's glasses, Professor. Take your time. Take your time, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we're ready to proceed, Mr. President, the witness has his spectacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may now ask the witness whether or not he has taken the time to read. Have you done so, Professor? Are you ready to respond to the question? Have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't understand the substance of the question. I can just tell you what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I am in the same position as you, Professor, I would like for the question to be repeated. Mr. Kehoe, please be very clear in your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The questions are quite unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's another issue. Mr. Kehoe, please, from the reading that has been done by the witness of this excerpt from this newspaper, would you please specify or clarify for these judges, which part of the interview you're targeting because I am not clear on that. What section are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 4, I believe. I believe on your copy, it's the middle of page 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have the English version here before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, we only have the English at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the issue. All right. Professor, we are on page 3. Mr. Kehoe, ask your question very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one point of clarification on that. This is at page 3 on the English translation. However, the doctor has before him a two-page article in BCS and for him it's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now we understand one another, please ask you question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you noted in an answer to a question several moments ago that you did not know what happened at these secret meetings in Karadjordjevo --

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you stated in this article in Nacional what Tudjman told you. And you noted -- you can read along with me -- at the beginning of 1991, following his negotiations with Milosevic, it was agreed that two commissions should meet and discuss a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tudjman then told us that he had made an agreement with Milosevic in principle and that we would have to work on the maps to work out the practical details. Did Tudjman tell you that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: As far as the Nacional is concerned I said yesterday that in the next issue of the Nacional that I denied part of the interpretations which I gave. That is the first point. Second, the journalists, some journalists tend to be very free when they make -- they give their titles. So, for example, in this Nacional, it states that I elaborated on a map on the division of Bosnia. That is of quite -- a very free interpretation, formulation by the journalist. A free formulation of the headlines to make the paper attractive to readers. But there is no document on that and I must say that Tudjman only spoke about the fact that on the basis of agreements of principle we should look into the possibilities. And we were to understand that we should just question the opposite side in the sense of their political goals for the forthcoming war. So Tudjman did not tell me that he had decided upon the division of Bosnia, but that he was looking into -- that he was asking the opposite side about their political goals. I said that yesterday, I repeat that here today and I think that state policy was different, which is borne out by the fact that the policies were realised, were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, is your testimony that Tudjman did not tell you that he had agreed with Milosevic in principle on the division of Bosnia; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That there should be negotiations with the opposite side as to how to treat Bosnia-Herzegovina. But a direct division of Bosnia in the sense that we have agreed to divide Bosnia along this line, that was absolutely never present in my talks with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go down two paragraphs in that article, in the article that's before you, 264. In the article, the paragraph that begins, "I warned Tudjman"... Do you see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "I warned Tudjman that there were three major obstacles to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that only one obstacle was enough for their agreement to fall through. First of all, the problem of deciding on Croatian and Serbian areas. Second, the problem of what the Muslims would say to everything." Tudjman replied that they would have nothing to say if Croats and Serbs agreed. I pointed out the third problem, which was not as serious as the first two, but still remained a problem. What will the International Community say to the agreement? Tudjman replied that the world would accept any agreement coming out of the region. Doctor, did you have that discussion with then President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Let me explain it to you. I said yesterday that I, together with a group of journalists in the Nacional, drank whiskey and discussed the topic. And on that occasion I explained these three obstacles as my own personal explanation, interpretation of that historical moment. And they gave this as if I had said it to President Tudjman. I spoke to the journalist as my vision and it was incorrectly quoted there. So I am the author of those theses, which I presented to the journalist as being my own thesis. I did not say that they were Tudjman's. They were my own; whereas they interpreted them as if I had told them that this was something that Tudjman had said -- as I had said to Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that you had filed a retraction on this article in the first of November 1996 edition of Nacional; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Two or three issues later, because the Nacional did not wish to publish my criticism. And what it did publish it once again left out a large portion of my answer. So that I had some polemics with the Nacional. When they received my reply, they promised to publish it in its entirety, but they failed to do so. Therefore, I consider that this discussion about newspaper articles is something that I, myself, could not stand behind because very often they are talks which one has with journalists and sometimes they have the aim, even for me personally, of placing something for the public for different reasons. And I don't like to speak about these things as a scientific worker myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The retraction does not retract the conversations that you had with Tudjman, does it?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I said, before your question, I said that part of the answer, my answer was not published. Part of my retraction was not published by the Nacional. They did not want to publish this and I said that before you asked your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, there are several photographs in that article of you, as well, are there not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I see two photographs of me here, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were those photographs taken in a barroom?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I can't remember. If I were to remember all these details, if one was to remember all the details of one's life, I don't know. It's impossible to know. I don't know where they got the photographs from. Perhaps they were taken at the editorial office. Perhaps they took it from one of their files, their records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the fact was that a Nacional reporter came and took those photographs of you for this article, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I repeat, I have already answered that question. I don't know whether they took the photographs then. It's impossible to recall all these details in life because had I been able to recall all these details, I would not be a scientific worker, I would be something else. Perhaps they took their documents then, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do not recall, Doctor, that the Nacional photographer came and took these photographs of you; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a moment please. Don't forget, I also have this. I need to maintain order in these proceedings. Mr. Nobilo, you have an objection. Please make your objection first and then I will say what I have to say about that matter. Please make your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, whether the photographs were taken then or were taken from the files, this question has been answered by the witness. So the Prosecutor is repeating the same question and is getting the same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please, I think you're saying, if I understand correctly, you're saying that you want us to respond in the place of the witness. If I understood that's your objection, then that's okay, that's sustained. Now, Mr. Kehoe, you've asked questions, the answer was given to you by the witness. The witness says he does not remember. That's fine. That's how it is. We're going to end on the issue of the Nacional newspaper. I believe he stated that there was a retraction, if I understand correctly. You stated that there was a retraction. Then, after that, it did not go as you wanted it to. The problem is not that issue there. But Mr. Kehoe, do you have any further questions you wish to put to the witness? Then I must remind the witness that when he responds to questions, he must respond facing the judges. It is not a dialogue between you and the prosecution. So, Mr. Kehoe, have you ended with this cross-examination dealing with the issue of what Mr. Tudjman stated and the interview regarding the Nacional newspaper? Please, go on, tell us how many more questions you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On this particular question, I am going to ask the witness to read the retraction, because I think it's important, given the context of this interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Mr. Nobilo, the retraction is part of the cross-examination. Do you have an objection on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, because the witness said that the retraction was published, but that an important portion of his retraction was left out by the newspaper and it didn't publish it. So I consider the question answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But your objection is not sustained. But the Prosecution I understand wanted to ask a question regarding the retraction and indeed that retraction is part of the interview, so what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question is Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to show this retraction to the doctor and ask him to identify it as the copy of the retraction that appeared in the 6th of November, 1996, edition of Nacional. I just got this this morning, given yesterday's testimony. I do not have a copy in either English or in French. I will ask the witness to read it into the record. I have provided copies of this retraction to the three respective booths. I believe everybody has it to assist it in their interpretation in English and in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that it is not proper for the witness to read the newspaper here now. It is not something that is customary in this court. The Prosecutor's office may read it and then the witness can confirm what is being read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps the witness may agree to read. So we can go faster. Professor, do you agree to read this document so that we can interpret it? Professor, I'm addressing you directly. Professor, do you agree to read this retraction in your language?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, each judge has the Serbo-Croatian version. Do the interpreters also have their copies of the retraction?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I see that they're saying yes. So I see that since the Professor agrees to read it -- Professor, please go on and read this article. It's not very long, and deals with your incomplete, as you have stated, retraction, but it is the retraction that you submitted and the one that is being presented to you by the Office of the Prosecutor. We are listening to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: My interview published in issue number 49 of the Nacional was not authorised, and in view of the trust that I have in journalist Mladen Plaset, I did not expect him to take such freedom in interpreting, literatise, licentia poetica my words. However, this has not substantially distorted what I said. The problem occurred after the interview was published, when talking over a drink, in addition to the two of us there were several other journalists with whom I conversed about various events. In the course of that conversation, I spoke about the year 1991, about the dramatic preparations for a military push, about Bosnia and Herzegovina within the framework of the overall Yugoslav crisis and Serbia's attitude towards that republic. In conversations of this kind, one spontaneously mixes reminiscences with present-day views of things, so that an interpretation emerged with is not authentic and some points in it are not even truthful. This applies, in particular, to Generals Trgo and Kukoc. Namely, prior to the military intervention in Slovenia, I travelled from Zagreb to Belgrade two or three times and talked to several people. The Federal Prime Minister Anto Markovic, the Foreign Minister Budimir Loncar, the previous Prime Minister of the Federal Government Branko Vikolic, the Serbian writer Dobrica Cofic, men in the Central Committee of the Legal Communists of Yugoslavia, as well as several retired generals, among whom were these two above named. From all these conversations, as well as all the rumours going around Belgrade, one could conclude that the military would not watch quietly and indifferently the dramatic debates in the presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic at the time, but that they were preparing for a military intervention. Therefore, Generals Trgo and Kukoc were not my source of information, but I learnt from the information from the talks I had with these people. Unfortunately, in the shortened version of the interview, the names of several other senior officers of the JNA were left out, so that only the names of Trgo and Kucic remained, as if they had announced the intervention, which is quite incorrect. The same can be said about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Namely, in that story, there was an intermingling of information and my subsequent experiences and present-day views in connection with those events. I claim categorically that mostly the Avnoj borders were discussed, the borders between the former republics of Yugoslavia, where as a result of a fierce argument broke out in which I defended those borders while the Serbs attacked them as the work of two Croats, that is Tito and Subasic, who were Prime Ministers of two parallel Yugoslavia governments, Tito of the Partisan Government and Subasic of the Royal Government. Of course, the Serbs those added to those the names the names of Kardelj, and the pre-war Comintern policy of breaking up of Yugoslavia, all of which was intended to serve as the basis of their main thesis that those borders cannot be accepted. That was how this conversation turned into a kind of round-table, rather like the round-table discussions that historians have. I claim categorically that I did not see maps on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For me as a historian, and a chronicler of the time in which we live, it was a challenge to participate in those debates which gave me an opportunity to link the present with history, and that was the main thing. The time will come when this issue will re-emerge and then historiographic elaboration of a problem will be made. This is all. May I add to this that what is written here is what I said. First, that we were discussing things over a drink; secondly, that there was an intermingling of current reports with my own reflections and thoughts; so that an interview was produced from which it is not possible to draw the conclusion that a division had been ordered or agreed, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You may now, Mr. Kehoe, ask one question regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, this retraction contains no retraction concerning your discussions with President Tudjman, does it?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have three or five times already said that my retraction was not published in its entirety and I do not understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I've taken note of that, Professor. Mr. Kehoe, the witness has stated -- he says five times, but nonetheless, he said that his retraction had the not been fully published in its full version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, after these secret meetings that you participated in in Tikves, you withdrew from these discussions concerning the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you, because you did not approve of them?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I withdrew because I had achieved what I had wanted to achieve as a historian. Of course, I did not agree during this overall situation at the time already. I had the feeling that chaos and turmoil would ensue. And I withdrew for a number of reasons, not only the one that you are alleging, but I felt that the whole issue was not clear, it had not been defined, that I didn't really know what the politicians wanted on either side, and that myself as a scholar, as a professional, had no place there because the policies were contradictory. On the one hand, there was a firm decision to defend the republican borders. On the other hand there was talks going on which I was not familiar with, state, parastatal talks, I don't know. So there were several reasons why I gave up my participation in that undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the talks continued, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, because that group of experts fell apart, or was disbanded, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you testified, did you not, several weeks ago in the case of Prosecutor -- versus Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please ask your question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I simply asked the witness whether or not he testified in that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suppose if you're asking the question then you must know that he was present. At least I hope the Office of the Prosecutor knows already. So please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, in that particular discussion, Doctor, you noted that, "I resigned from the continuation of the talks." And then you went on to note, "Q. In no way do I imply any criticism of you," this is by the Prosecutor, "I am merely endeavouring to elicit -- eliciting the facts. But the fact of the matter is that following the meeting between Tudjman and Milosevic, you were assigned as a member of this commission to endeavour to reach an agreement with the Serbs on the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that your concern at that time was the fate of the Muslims." The answer is, "Yes. As soon as I saw what was happening, from a kind of historical curiosity I accepted to take part in the talks." And later on you say, "I cannot say what happened afterwards because the contacts probably continued." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The word "probably" is something I wish to underline, because interstate contacts between Belgrade and Zagreb were constant, diplomatic, non-diplomatic of various kinds. It's quite logical that contacts and links were not totally interrupted, but I personally do not know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, is it your belief that after your departure from those talks that those talks concerning the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: My belief is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Nobilo. It seems that the question has been asked already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has quite clearly said, on several occasions, that he has no knowledge about what happened later. Therefore, the grounds for this question do not exist, because the witness has said that he doesn't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you might rephrase your question unless -- we're going to be going on to the break. Do you have another question about these meetings in Karadjordjevo, if so, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President. The witness has answered the question as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Do you have many more questions in your cross-examination, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, Your Honour. I would say probably an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to take our first break of ten minutes. We're going to reconvene at 20 minutes to the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you resigned from this commission because you did the not accept the concepts about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you disagreed with what was happening, so as a Communist of 50 years you left; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I have already answered that question, adding the fact that the situation was so complicated that I didn't consider myself competent to continue to be involved in a dramatic situation, so that I have already answered that question and explained what I have just added.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 225, at line 20 of your prior testimony in Aleksovski, you noted, "I publicly came out against the radicalism, both Serb and Croatian, because as I know, for 50 years I was a Communist, and I don't accept the concepts about the division, so that's why I resigned." Now, that was your testimony in the Aleksovski case, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes. I was always in favour of moderate policies and against radical ones, because I myself went through the radical policies of the revolution, socialist revolution, and I had had enough of this radicalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you did not agree with the policies of division that President Tudjman advocated, did you, as it pertained to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I didn't claim that, and I claim today that I'm not sure of that, because it wasn't explicitly stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be divided, but that the overall situation should be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, in early 1994, President Tudjman called upon you to go to Belgrade as a representative of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned colleague, but in our examination-in-chief, we reached as far as the break-up of Yugoslavia, that is 1990. About the years that followed and the duties of this witness in '93, '94, in the independent Republic of Croatia is something we did not discuss, so this is quite outside the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will tell the Court exactly the question that I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Finish with your question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, you were called upon to go to Serbia as a representative for the Republic of Croatia as part of a reconciliation mission with the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to leaving, you had a discussion with President Tudjman in early 1994, where he said, "I know that you do not agree with my policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did he not say that to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Hold on. Before the witness responds to that question, I would first like to see whether or not the Judges would like for this question to be put under Rule 70. The Rules of Procedure give the Judges the right to put a question -- rather, under Rule 90, the Judges do have indeed the right to put a question to the witness. First let me consult with my colleagues. The Trial Chamber -- and this will also account for the following questions, deems that Rule 90 does indeed -- rather, 98, dealing with additional evidence presented by the witness, the Trial Chamber may order either party to produce additional evidence, and it may, if appropriate, summon witnesses and order their attendance, but in this case the Judges do have the right to give the Defence the right to re-examine on issues which are not covered in examination-in-chief. Mr. Kehoe, you may ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, in this discussion with President Tudjman in early 1994, he said to you, "I know that you, Dr. Bilandzic, do not agree with my policy in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And that was the policy of a division in Bosnia-Herzegovina that you didn't agree with; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I really cannot remember that I said that, and even if I did say that it had been said, I simply cannot remember that. I did not hear such a statement from president Tudjman, even if it was published in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we should like to learn the source from which the Prosecutor is quoting. Secondly, we would like to have a copy, because it seems to me that the Prosecutor has added his own interpretation to this quotation. If allegedly President Tudjman said, "I know that you do not agree with my policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina," and then the Prosecutor added, "That was the division of Bosnia, wasn't it?" So I think this is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's be very clear. You mentioned quotations. Would you please give us the source, otherwise, it would seem that you're giving an interpretation of what the witness had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The source is, again, Exhibit 264, the newspaper article from Nacional, and on the second to last page, and in the area, Doctor, if you can look the at Exhibit 264 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 464 is it not, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge, 464.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you see, Doctor, in the area on the -- I believe it's your second page, starting with "Free agent"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please underline where that sentence is, Mr. Kehoe? I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the English version it's on page 6. If I can point to it, Your Honour, it's right here. On page 6. I realise this is a rather unscientific method, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Riad has placed it before me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you said in this article in Nacional that President Tudjman said to you you do not agree with my policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina but it would be good if you went to Belgrade. Do you see that quote?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: What it says here is -- I should like to repeat what I already said. I can't find it here, but I don't think that is important, Your Honours, because I do not absolutely recall Tudjman saying that to me, and we have already spoken about this sufficiently, that is, that I protested with the Nacional, saying that it had misinterpreted many of my thoughts, and I cannot recall President Tudjman saying that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, place us in time and help us with this, Doctor. You were recalled from Belgrade in May of 19595; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you had spent 15 months in Belgrade on this diplomatic mission?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So any invitation by President Tudjman for you to undertake this diplomatic mission would have taken place in late 1993 or possibly early 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: You're thinking of when the mission was suspended, the agreement was more or less tête-à-tête that I would go to Belgrade for only a few months because I had retired and I had my own obligations with respect to writing books and I stayed for longer than originally had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the undertaking per the request of President Tudjman, was made to you by President Tudjman in the, say, last half of 1993; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, this was about 15 days prior to my departure for Belgrade. That was my first contact when I learned that he would like me to go to Belgrade, maybe 10 days before I actually left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So help me out here, Doctor, I am just trying o tie down the time frame here for the purposes of the record. If you came back in May of 1995, and you were there for 15 months, you must have had this discussion in late December 1993 or early January of 1994, unless my math is wrong; is that approximately right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I am repeating. Ten days or so prior to leaving for Belgrade, I was called to go on that mission, nothing more than that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And prior to that time, you had expressed disapproval, publicly you had expressed disapproval of the policies of the Republic of Croatia as it pertained to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; did you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't know what source you are referring to and what kind of non-approval you are referring to, what you mean as a member of the opposition. Ever since the first day of the establishment of the independent state of Croatia, I was a member of the presidency on behalf of the opposition and to this day I am a member of the opposition. And as a member of an opposition party, I often spoke critically about the regime because that is the logic of a political opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I guess we'll go into this in a little more detail, Doctor. You wrote a book that we talked about yesterday, where you criticised the establishment of the Kninska Krajina, because it established a state within a state of the Republic of Croatia and, as such, presented an intolerable situation for the Republic of Croatia; do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, the League of Communists of Croatia of whose central committee I was a member, from the first day of the conflict with Milosevic's policies, always pursued a policy of defence of Croatia and it remains that that policy remains in force to this day. And within the framework of that policy, I was naturally against this so-called Balvan Revolution or Log Revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that revolution started as a cultural grouping and ultimately turned into I believe what you described yesterday as an entity that had all the trappings of statehood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No, that is not right. On the 19th of July, 1990, the people of Knin took up arms. They cut wood. They put up obstacles to block traffic between Croatia and its coastline. They blocked the main road and the conflict started immediately there. Cultural autonomy was just a way of legitimising the so-called Balvan Revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for objecting again. Of course the Defence appreciates the right of the Trial Chamber to call for evidence of its own, but it appears -- we would just like the time that is being used for this not to be counted as the Defence time as this is quite outside the examination-in-chief and, therefore, it is based on a different grounds than the regular cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are not incorrect. But we would like to see whether the Prosecution has further questions which is of great interest to the Chamber and to the judges. Please understand, Mr. Nobilo, that when you have a witness who is very close to those in power in a historical and a political knowledge that also interests the judges a great deal. Now I turn to Mr. Kehoe to see whether this cross-examination which you are carrying out with questions, which, once again, I repeat, the judges find of great interest must nonetheless ask the question about the time. Are you in agreement with that, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge. I mean, if the Court wants to suspend the time against the Defence on that score, the Prosecution has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Our records indicate that about 30 minutes was within the scope and the rest of the examination has focused on personal contacts with President Tudjman and the witness' views about policies of the Republic of Croatia after the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. President, with that analysis is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I propose to be flexible. We, the judges, have stated that on the Rule of 98 that these questions can be of interest to the Blaskic case. However, you do, indeed, have the right to re-examination. If indeed time has been taken from you, you will not sacrifice your right to re-examination. That will be granted to you. But, nonetheless, please do not abuse this flexibility that we are showing. This witness is here. He has also appeared in other cases. He was a very important political agent in the events that took place in that area. We understand you have many questions for you. However, please do not digress in your questions, please do not multiply them, backtrack, otherwise we have great difficulty in understanding what questions you are asking. Please put your questions directly and please try to make strong efforts in this area. We do not want to have any further incidents as we have seen just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, going directly to the point. Yesterday in your testimony, you were strongly opposed to the establishment of the Republic of Serb Krajina as it was the establishment of a state within the state of a Republic of Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also, sir, were strongly opposed to the activities that led to the establishment of the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna and the ultimate creation of the Republic of Herzeg-Bosna, were you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, the idea about establishing Herzeg-Bosna itself until the process was completed, I was not included and cannot testify as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That particular movement, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, we have asked you whether or not you were against it or not. This is a question which is of interest to the judges. We've asked you whether you yourself were against it. If you do not answer the question now, I can tell you that right now I, myself, will ask you that question. So please try to respond to that question now or in a moment. It's a question which id very clear. Yes or no, were you against the creation of the Herzeg-Bosna community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Herzeg-Bosna was created, then I came to learn that it had been established and that is why I did not assume a public stand because about the initiative and the process of creating Bosnia-Herzegovina -- Herzeg-Bosna, I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you knew, doctor, that the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna, when it was established on the 18th of November, 1991, had a goal of becoming a part of the Republic of Croatia; did you not learn that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know where the source comes from because I did not have any decided stands on Herzeg-Bosna and I had retired from political life already at the time and I did not participate in this. So I have no stand on Herzeg-Bosna here until it was already formed. I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you do know, doctor, that the goals of the Croatia community of Herzeg-Bosna were annexation with the Republic of Croatia; you do know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No, I don't know the source that I knew that Herzeg-Bosna should be annexed to Croatia. I don't know where the source comes from. That is, that I knew about this and that I was against it or anything about it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you perceived that that creation of the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna, was an effort to divide the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was a live process which began, which lasted in its ultimate goal. What it was to be, I did not know of it, nor could I have known. And I always took the view that the constituents of each nation be respected. And I never said decidedly anything about Herzeg-Bosna, so I don't know the source of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move ahead, Doctor. You believe and concluded as a historian that after the establishment of the Vance-Owen Plan that the authorities in Herzeg-Bosna had concluded that they could do what they wanted; didn't you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Not quite like that. I condemned, that is to say I have not got the right to condemn, but I stated, I said that I considered that neither the Republic of Srpska or Herzeg-Bosna should have the position which would lead towards a definite division. I said this on several occasions, but in precise terms, my own policy, my own positions, I did not declare, but I did say that I did not consider it to be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You concluded that the granting of Bosnian Croats citizenship in the Republic of Croatia was a mistake, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Perhaps I just noted that it had been done, but I did not qualify this either as a mistake or as a good thing either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also concluded that representation by Bosnian Croats in the Sabor was also a mistake; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't know where you have the resource that it was a mistake. But I was against the fact -- let me be more precise. I supported, but I do not have a stand on this, nor did I ever have a stand. I never said anything about the matter of representation. But, intimately, I thought that this was not the right solution. I don't remember saying anything or writing anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, when you're going to be citing something, I hope that you will name the source if you're going to quote from some document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, Doctor, your positions were consistent, you were against the formation of the Kninska Krajina, within the Republic of Croatia in the same way that you were against the establishment of the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna and the Republic of Herzeg-Bosna because it would lead to the break up of individual republics; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In principle, I assumed that stand, but when the Prosecutor, Your Honours, say that I expressly stated, then this is a mistake. I don't recall having expressly stated this. Because a mistake is that kind of qualification. It can mean one thing or another. They're all relative matters. And taking part in political life, particularly when you're a member of the opposition, one allows oneself the right to overdimensionalise in order to make it difficult for the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, this is a question of methodology. I think you must respect the rigorous principles of methodology. Either you ask the witness his opinion and then the witness will give his opinion. Or, you should list the facts and then ask him to comment on those. You cannot pile on questions, approximative questions, you, it seems, did so and so. And then end that with a question by saying, therefore, if you're against such and such a thing. Do you follow me? Do you follow what problem I have? Is it a question of methodology in your questioning. This is a procedure that must be followed. Either you ask the opinion of the witness. That is your absolute right. But, you should not start off with a question from which the answer is already there. Then, derive a certain answer from that. And this is an intellectual exercise which is not very clear. So please make an effort in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, do you know a reporter by the name of Jasmina Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you give an interview or comment to her on the 21st of July, or it was published on the 21st of July, 1993, on a wire service known as "Associative Press"?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That is possible, Your Honours. I had interviews with hundreds and hundreds of journalists. Now, whether I gave this particular person an interview, I don't have records on this in my personal documents or anywhere, so I don't remember. I don't know the sense of the question. The question is not a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, let me get more direct on the question. During the midst of the war between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, did you express your displeasure of the policies of the Republic of Croatia in saying if one divides Bosnia, why shouldn't one divide Croatia? It's a logical consequence. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It can possibly be stated, but I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now here's a question of methodology once again. You have that article, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do, I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You don't even know what the date of the article is. So, please, when you have an article, please specify which article you are referring to, otherwise we will lose a great deal of time. I don't even have the year. So, please, you can say you gave to such and such a paper on such and such and date and then we can end with that and the witness can tell you what he feels, what he thinks about that. Let's continue on that vein Mr. Kehoe, but not to keep going around the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. President, I do believe I led in before the question that this was an article that was published approximately on the 21st of July, 1993 by an Associative Press reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You do not recall giving that particular interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I have at least 2.000 pages of interviews and who can remember an interview, particularly in that dramatic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, Doctor, during July of 1993, did you believe that the Croatians were attempting to divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is also a strange question. My stand of principle was always to retain the results of the partisan war. That is to say, this republic. And it is from those positions that I always defended these stands. And then, of course, in one or another interview, following a policy of that kind, and as I was a member of the opposition, I could have said one thing or another. So whether I thought one thing or another is difficult for me to say. I cannot define it. I cannot remember precisely what exactly I said in July 1993, what I thought in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then, maybe we can refresh your recollection, Doctor, by going to the second clip and I believe that's 463-B, if I am not mistaken, Mr. Dubuisson. If we can play that next clip again. Again this is another excerpt from dispatches. Excuse me, video room, can you start that from the beginning with the volume, please. And the lights, please, if you could dim the lights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall that interview, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Well, the question, as a member of the opposition party, of course I remember. I wanted to explain and I was close to the view that this was a state of fact. And from that state of fact to politics and what should be done is a long road, a large step to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you conclude that the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna was attempting to establish a state within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I only took note of what had been done. I did not conclude anything. My statement talks about what they did within their territorial unit. And I have no stand there, what they were thinking of doing in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In any event, Doctor, you concluded that the Croats from Herzegovina thought that the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was done and that they could do whatever they wanted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Well, you used a bit of licentia poetica there. I did not say that, poetic licence. It was a dramatic process which was ongoing and it was to end later on according to the logics of recognition because Croatia was later to recognise, not later, but it definitely recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina and an organisation within Herzeg-Bosna was both military and political because at that time in the aggressive war against the JNA and Serbia and so on and so forth, something had to be done in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Doctor, let me go back for one moment before we conclude. In your paper that you wrote, "Croatian Between War and Independence." A paper that was published by the University of Zagreb in 1991. And in your conclusion, you state the following thing: "Criminal deeds go hand in hand with criminal lies. This is an old and often proven truth." Doctor, do you believe that today as much as you believed that in 1991?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, criminal deeds go hand in hand with what? I don't understand the sense of the sentence. It alludes me. If I wrote it, then the interpretation is completely unclear and the Prosecutor's interpretation is unclear. What does it mean? Criminal deeds are criminal deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
