utterances.text: I will read it for you one more time. And I quote as follows on page 90 of your book: "Criminal deeds go hand in hand with criminal lies. This is an old and often proved truth." Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Even if I did write it, I think that it is a little -- that it has two meanings and it is not sufficiently clear. A criminal deed, something has to precede criminal deeds and you lawyers know that. You have to have intent beforehand or some sort of action, preparation for some thing. And criminal lies, it states that criminal lies are also criminal deeds. Is that the sense of the question? Whether I consider that lies are criminal deeds? It is not a very clear sentence and I doubt that I could have written a sentence which lacked clarity of that kind. Or perhaps it is a question of translation. I don't understand the exact sense, either of the sentence or the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The sentence does not go on too much further. Otherwise it seems that we are arriving at a paradoxical situation, where the author of the sentence would have to receive an explanation from someone else about that sentence means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we have it in the native language in which it was written, the witness can see it. If we have it in BSC, Your Honour, that might cut through the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We have a possible difficulty. I understand the witness to be reacting to a proposition which says that a criminal lie is a criminal deed. The sentence which was quoted to you was, however, a little different. That criminal deeds go hand in hand with criminal lies. From that, there is no necessary inference, criminal lies are always criminal deeds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours, with that interpretation made by the judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you Judge Shahabuddeen having clarified that issue. Mr. Kehoe, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I do not. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Nobilo. Now, you realise the re-examination should be within the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That's right. But I suppose with additional questions I could enter into a new cross-examination outside the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In any event, Professor please explain to the Court whether there is a difference in expressing assertions in a political struggle and presenting assertions in a scientific work, including professional expertise given before this Criminal Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, absolutely. Because statements, Your Honours, in a political struggle, are something that is aimed at having your political adversary disqualified. And when we're talking about science, then the approach must be quite different. The methods might be quite different and the statements different. And I assume that this holds true in a court of law as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly in saying that the weight and precision and quality of one, that is statements said in the heat of political argument, and a different weight is placed on something that you, as a scientist, write or state or something which you, as a scientist, state before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The ethics of science has its own ethics and political struggles have their own ethics which are different according to my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are a member of the strongest opposition party in the Republic of Croatia and whether it is -- is it the aim of your opposition party to overthrow president Tudjman's power and party, of course, in a parliamentary manner?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I think I can confirm this because the whole meaning of having an opposition party is to come into power one day. And, of course, in Croatia this means by parliamentary methods today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You -- we heard mention of the Nacional a lot of times, is this a pro-government newspaper or anti-government newspaper?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: It's expressly opposition anti-government and expressly critical. And I always follow the Nacional and I must say, unfortunately, that I don't very often agree with them because at times they overstep the code of conduct and morals -- well, not morals, that's a little heavy, but they overstep the frameworks of Buto in order to inflict a blow to the regime and the ruling party. And I have the impression I could also supply you with documents because I myself am convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In a young democracy, such as Croatia, is that the characteristic of the majority of newspapers?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Also in this case I think, Your Honours, this is a broad question. But I must say one thing and that is that the mentality that reigns the Mediterranean mountainous mentality in polemics does not always take care of content and style, but very often they react very sharply and heatedly. In Croatia we have several newspapers who are in the forefront of this kind of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would the Nacional, do you assess that the Nacional is also politically oriented like your own party as an opposition in the direction of overthrowing the existing powers that are in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, it's far more critical than my own party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Croatia, in our political discussions there, when we speak of division, the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does this encompass a division within the state, that is who is going to be dominant in power within? And the same term, is it used in the division of the same state into two, three or more parts? Am I right in saying the same term, "division", is used for breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina and also when we mean division in the local division of government within Bosnia-Herzegovina? Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Well, I think that politics and the processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the first day to the present, are such that the term "division" is really used both for a policy of Bosnia as an entirety, that is that the division must ensure constituency of the three basic elements. Those who wish to have the division of Bosnia also use the same term "division". So this is rather a confusing term, a confusion of terms, terms which are not quite clear, and daily politics uses, intentionally, these confusing terms, both the ruling party and the opposition parties use this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In concrete terms, is Bosnia divided into two ethnicities today -- entities in keeping with the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Well, the Dayton Accords, in fact, divided Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the opposition overemphasises this assessment, that the International Community divided Bosnia and that it now keeps it divided. This is particularly widespread, the accepted widespread view in the opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, from -- we discussed Karadjordjevo a great deal, so I won't dwell on that, but you said that you did not see any document from a meeting in Karadjordjevo, and that President Tudjman did not tell you the contents of the talks there.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now I'm asking you whether anybody -- any other member of the Croatian delegation who was present in Karadjordjevo told you about the contents of the talks in Karadjordjevo between the representatives of Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Neither the Minister, nor the Prime Minister, nobody told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So just with one sentence, can we definitely conclude and discard all doubt that you have no knowledge on the talks in Karadjordjevo and what was discussed in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tikves. You said that the meeting in Tikves boiled down to a discussion on whether the boarders from the Second World War can or cannot be changed. Can you tell me in precise terms whether this related to the external borders of Yugoslavia or the republican borders?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your question -- even in my interview in the Nacional, says that -- and that is the frequently quoted Nacional is an important source here, that practically the entire talks were -- evolved in a polemics as to which borders were meant. The talks gave me the impression, a strong impression, that both sides, in discussing borders, understood that they were dealing exclusively with internal borders, because none of the sides brought into question external borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Professor, could you please make it clear to the court; in our political terminology, when we say "internal borders," do we have in mind the borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Absolutely, completely. There is no dilemma there. We have in mind exclusively the republican borders, which according to the 1974 constitution, were defined as the boarders of the states of the republics. So state borders are borders -- internal borders between the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Having said that, may we conclude, in view of your previous statement, that you, together with the other representatives from Croatia, advocated no change for the boarders of Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: While I took part in those talks the answer is yes, and after me and before me I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To objectvise the situation, at that time -- in that time span, that is the armed insurrection of the Serbs in Krajina, which brought into question Croatian state borders, Croatia could allow itself the political luxury of bringing into question its internal borders within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The political-military-international situation in the early spring of 1991 was such that it reached a climax. That is to say, it was the time when preparations for a military coup were being prepared, and when the Minister of the army went to the Soviet Union, to Marshal Jasov (Phoen), and Croatia found itself in a situation which was a difficult one, so difficult that any serious policy, anybody serious at the time would not have opened a front of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have heard you were an expert working with the peaks of Croatian power and authority during the disintegration period of Yugoslavia. Now, I ask you the following: At that time, or afterwards, and we're now entering into the region, right up to the present day, whether you ever saw one official document of the Republic of Croatia which would demand, request, the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: As far as I know, a document of that kind does not exist. I had occasion to look at the documents of our Sabor, or parliament, of the government, of the Foreign Affairs Ministry, as far as I was able through the mass media, and as far as I know I don't know of any document of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have asked you officially. Did you see a secret document of the organs of Croatia seeking for this division?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court what state in the world first recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I think that it was Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the diplomatic world, when a state is recognised, what does that mean in view of its territory and borders?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: It means that the side recognises the integrity of the country recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: It means that in the case of Yugoslavia and recognition of mutual -- whether Serbia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina Montenegro, whatever, that the signing and the international recognition meant recognition of its existing borders. That is political practice. And that holds true for Slovenia, with which we do have diplomatic relations. It holds true for Macedonia and also for Serbia, although -- that is to say Yugoslavia. Although with Yugoslavia, we have the problem of the Prehlika (Phoen) area, that although that is a specific issue. However, Yugoslavia and Croatia recognised existing borders, and existing borders are always recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Without side-stepping, did Croatia recognise Bosnian borders?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is recognition by the Republic of Croatia of Bosnia, was that before or after Karadjordjevo or can you remember?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Karadjordjevo was while Yugoslavia existed as an internationally recognised state. Therefore, we could not have spoken at that time. It was, let's say, one year before the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and nine months or eight months prior to the international recognition of Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and four months prior to the beginning of the war. So we're dealing here with Yugoslavia, which was still an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, Professor, the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina by Croatia came after Karadjordjevo. That's what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, one year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now tell me, in relation to Karadjordjevo, how much time elapsed before the Great War broke out between Serbia, the JNA and Croatia? How long after Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From the moment of the meeting in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. From Karadjordjevo to the outbreak of war between Serbia and Croatia, how much time elapsed?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: About four months. Yes, about four months later. The real war began in the summer of 1991, and up until then, there were outbreaks in Krajina, Knin. Clashes existed in Pakrac, Dalj and so on and so forth. These were clashes that broke out. But a frontal attack by the JNA began on Croatia from Serbia in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Professor. You have a great deal of scientific, political and every other kind of experience, so could you tell the Court, as a historian, as a politician, what do you conclude from the fact that the war broke out after Karadjordjevo, a war in which the large town of Croatia was destroyed, Vukovar, the holy place of Croatia at Dubrovnik and so on? What do you conclude from that fact, that the war broke out four months after the meeting in Karadjordjevo? What is your conclusions regarding what happened or did not happen in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a very interesting question to which history will certainly be able to provide an answer, but it is self-explanatory, without going into a thorough analysis, that a bloody war between two parties should not have occurred if those opposing parties had reached some kind of a mutual agreement. Because if there was an agreement, then there's no way to explain why the war broke out, because as is known, the war was indeed bloody. The JNA had about 15.000 killed soldiers and 40.000 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On whose side?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: On the side of Croatia. And about ten towns were destroyed. So it is quite incomprehensible that such a brutal and bloody war could have occurred after any kind of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, 15.000 dead, 30- to 40.000 wounded and about ten destroyed towns after Tudjman and Milosevic had agreed on everything, according to you that is absurd?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that is all.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make a request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor. We are going to have a break now before the Judges will be asking you questions. Would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that my wife is very sick, and I have plane tickets for tomorrow morning. If perhaps you could devote a little more time to me today, I have to go back urgently, because I've been told today that my wife has to go into hospital for treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You are right to point that out, Professor, but I believe that after the break we will finish with the questions from the Judges. So you will be free to go as of this evening. We'll stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I neglected to offer the exhibits that I discussed during my cross-examination into evidence and with the Court's permission, I would like to do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We would like to ask the Prosecutor to specify which exhibits and documents he is referring to because he used a variety of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The video, I presume, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The video is broken down into 463 A and 463 B. The article, the Nacional article of the 25th of October, 1996, is 464 and 464 A and the retraction of which there is only a BCS version is 465. Those are the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. They have been admitted as numbered. Is that right, registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, we are now coming close to our conclusion, but now the judges have questions for you. I will now give the floor to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Indeed, I listen with great interest to your testimony which is of great historical dimension and I wish I could listen much more and read you more, I hope. Just a few things I need clarification in my mind in what you said. One of them interests me in particular, not only with regard to your testimony, it is the rights which you mentioned, the rights of a nation could be based on ethnic principle or could be based on national ethribution or based on history. And you seem to identify the ethnic principle with the principle of national ethribution and you said ethribution is tantamount to self-determination. I would like more clarification because I thought the ethnic principle is more linked with race. Is that what you meant that ethnic principle can be the basis of a nation or has it a wider scope? Is my question clear? Concerning the ethnic principle, what did you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Your Honour, in European theory of a nation is a social community comprising several elements. It should have several elements: Language, culture, history, and, in particular and most importantly, an individual feeling of a certain person, the conviction of that person that he belongs to a certain nation. I distinguish nation from race because I don't like the term race. But if we were to accept it in the conventional and popular sense, then within a race, there may be several nations. For instance, though this is not my strong point. For instance, among Arabs, there may be 10 nations. Among the Slavs who are not a race, but a large social grouping, there are about 10 states. So nation is something narrower. And nation according to European criteria can no longer be subdivided. It remains a whole. As for the principle of self-determination, this is a political category, which may or may not be allowed to a nation to resort to, that is to self-determine itself. According to Stalin's policy, for instance, this right to self-determination was not recognised until the Soviet Union was disintegrated. As for these two terms: Ethnic is national; ethnos, that is belonging to a particular situation, an ethnos becomes a nation when it becomes conscious of definite political goals. The ethnic principle is the principle for the formation of nations, but the historical principle is one that I do not recognise. In other words, I do not recognise the right of, for instance, former empires because they used to govern certain peoples, have the right to gain control of those peoples again. Though any right may be abused, including the right to self-determination, as well as the right to historical borders. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both of the two larger nations ought, or to be more precise, both Croatia and Serbia over a period of 150 years equally claimed the right over Bosnia-Herzegovina in the name of the ethnic and in the name of the historical right. I don't know whether I have been of any assistance. Therefore, in Europe, you have nations such as the German nation, the French nation, the Russian nation, the Italian nation, the Croatian nation, the Hungarian nation. Those are nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just to go to your last affirmation. When you said Croatia and Serbia are claiming rights over Bosnia based on ethnic principle and on historical ground, what is the historical ground? And what is the ethnic principle in this instance?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That tendency is 150 years old. It emerged in the middle of the 19th century as an idea and a tendency, as a plan, as a project. The starting point was that both parties believed that the Muslims were actually Slavs, but they were Serbs or, in the other case, Croats. Both parties proceeded from the belief that they are of a certain faith. Because, when the Muslims came into being, there were no nations in Europe at the time in the sense in which that concept was established with the French Revolution. When Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1500 something was captured by the Turks, all was that they found there were Slavs of Catholic faith and Orthodox faith. And then later on, national ideologues said that the Muslims who converted to Islam were exclusively Catholics. That would be one theory in Croatia. In Serbia, Karadzic and other theoreticians claim that they were all Orthodox who converted to Islam. Therefore, they remained Serbs, but they only changed their religion, which scientifically cannot be proven quite precisely because the social consciousness in the middle ages differed substantially from social consciousness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: At least the fact remains, the bottom line is that they were Slavs? The Bosnians were Slavs?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They are sometimes called Turks, is that a right description?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That is true too. But they changed ethnically, although I do not know their history very well. But during the Osmanly Rule, Turks did settle in Bosnia and in time they came to recognise themselves as Turks, as Bosniaks, as something rather vague, so that the research done so far into this issue are quite lacking, even though all three parties have their own interpretations, today's Bosniaks, former Muslims and the Serbs and the Croats each have their own versions about the situation as it was in the middle ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is the version of the Bosniaks themselves?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The version of the Bosniaks, I will be referring to contemporary views. The Bosnian Muslims always considered themselves a separate people. And when nations were being formed, the nations of the Croatian and the Serbian nation, they took the position that, or they aspired towards becoming an autochthonous factor and that tendency was weak because some of them really did consider themselves Serbs and other Croats, but as of the end of the 19th century, and especially with the formation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and Tito's socialist Yugoslavia, they tended increasingly to see themselves as a separate national unit. And the Constitution of Yugoslavia recognised this for the first time this figured in the population census of Yugoslavia in 1971. Therefore, today, they have definitely become a formed national community which has this national consciousness of being a separate nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your information. Just another question which comes to my mind and you are not obliged to answer it. When you spoke of the negotiations in Kresovo between President Tudjman and President Milosevic, you just said that it was on how to treat Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did you mean by "How to treat Bosnia"? What does the meaning of "How to treat?" Did you have a definition or rather an explanation of it?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: As I did not get completely clear and precise instructions or information that indeed it had to do with a division, something I didn't believe in, but let me say in passing, I saw that assignment as a political drive conducted before the war. The aim of which was to test the enemy, which from whom one expected the war to start, to see the views regarding that problem. And, secondly, to gain time. However, as intimately I favoured an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know when one personally believes in something, he is not prone to accept such directives. But I can claim with emphasis that I received no document about the Karadjordjevo meeting, nor was I orally told that, except to the effect that we should test what the views of Serbia were regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina and to see the possibility of coming to some kind of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor Bilandzic, as the president has told you, the Tribunal is not a college of historians and we are grateful to you for coming forward to help us. I shall be sufficiently prudent, I hope, not to enter into areas which are really beyond my reach. So I will ask you just one or two questions and let me begin with Mr. Djilas. Were you referring to the prominent Yugoslav writer?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, who was also a politician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He had more than one dimension to his character. He was both politician and writer. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now as you can appreciate, the Bench has an interest in the Karadjordjevo meeting. I understand, perfectly I hope, the position which you have expressed. You heard of it, but you never saw anything and you're not in a position to say authoritatively what may or may not have happened at Karadjordjevo; am I right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would I be right, however, in supposing, Professor, that you would have heard stories circulating that the meeting at Karadjordjevo was about dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, there were such rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would you, Professor, as a scientific person, have thought that that was an important question?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you, sir, have felt that your scientific pursuits would at least have encouraged you, if not required you, to probe the nature of the alleged agreement?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: If I live for another five or six years, I am 75-years-old, I hope that in five or six years' time, I will learn not only about that, but a whole series of events. It is well-known that some events from the Roman times are being discovered today. Or, for instance, some discoveries are being made about the political and social life in the former Soviet Union and the former Yugoslavia, so that a time distance is required to be able to clearly, fairly and scientifically to analyse the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you then to mean that, yes, you recognised that this was a matter of importance which could properly engage the mind of a scientific historian, but you considered that a time factor in the material factor required a deferment of close examination in order to arrive at an objective appreciation of whatever may have happened?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you see, Professor -- well, I know you saw it. Would you like to recall the clip which you saw yesterday and today, television clip. I think you prepared on it. After you prepared and spoke, Mr. Letica also appeared on the television clip? Another person? Yes. Am I right in my recollection, I did not take down his words, but I recall him speaking about maps and dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall him speaking about those matters?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you ever see that clip before today?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I think it was shown in the programme, the break up of Yugoslavia, the BBC movie. And I did watch that BBC film. And I remember that he appeared in that film. And I can tell you, quite frankly, that any maps about a division, I never saw. Whether he knows anything about that, I never discussed that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that perfectly. You, yourself, have never had any knowledge of maps. But, looking at the television programme at the time, did you have any reason to think that he was not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The TV programme was done quite fairly and honestly and I omitted to mention throughout my testimony here that I joined political life in 1939. I joined the communist movement. The communist movement very emphatically, but very emphatically, accused the Serbian and Croatian bourgeois of dividing Bosnia. And ever since 1939 for some 50, 60 years, and even before that actually, the communists had an entirely different concept. In the war of 1941, they decided that Bosnia had to be an equal state, one of the federal units. And for us communists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, perhaps I should explain. I am not asking about your own position. I am only asking whether at the time you thought that Mr. Letica was not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: I can't give you a very clear answer. Because Letica too is not very clear. He said there were maps, but he did not say I saw those maps. And I never asked him, so I don't know. I just wanted to end by saying that we communists were very rigid and this entered our blood stream, the belief that Bosnia had to prevail, that it had to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand your position perfectly, Professor. May I ask you a supplementary question on this point. At the time when you saw this clip, did anyone in authority in Croatia come forward to assert that Mr. Letica was not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In Zagreb, there was no public debate in political and scientific circles about this programme, so that I didn't have the opportunity to hear what individuals or the public thought about this TV programme or specifically about Letica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, Professor, we know that from what you have said that you have objected for the reasons which you have given, was a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is your position. Would I be right in understanding you to mean that the fact that you objected to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, implied that you knew it was a plan to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina? That is what you objected to?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In political life in the mass media and in the public in general, the topic of Bosnia was constantly on the agenda. And I often reacted to this story about Bosnia-Herzegovina, saying that we have to abide by the 1974 constitution. But in concrete terms, I cannot say anything more than I have already said. I am a little tired too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand. And I wouldn't weary you too much. I am about to conclude in one or two more modest questions, if I may. The president may have his little quota to add -- I shouldn't say little, but he will have his quota to add, but I am sure he will take note of your desire to escape, shall we say. Now, you were, Professor, a member of the commission, the commission was established formerly by law, by proclamation, by edict, how was it set up?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The term used was not a commission, but an expert group, which was to question the other side as to its intentions regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina and generally to get an idea of the strategy. In those dramatic circumstances, which were extremely dramatic, and the war was impending, and we needed to know what the other protagonists in the drama were thinking, and in that context this was this talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Were there any terms of reference of the expert group?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: No. Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the commission encountered some difficulties which you have explained. Were those difficulties related to the principle of dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did they relate to difficulties arising from implementation of the principle of dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: The question is a very good one and most inspiring, even for my future reflections. Psychologically, mentally, whichever way you want me to put it, we were obsessed with the problem of the totality of the political conflict on the soil of the former Yugoslavia, and our attention focused -- we were simply -- I can't find the right word. We were so preoccupied with the problem of whether we would emerge from an impossible situation, or would blood flow in streams. And for this reason the expert group focused on the problems of Yugoslavia as a whole. First we needed to resolve the question of Yugoslavia as a whole, and we will solve it if we stick to the rule that the republics are states and thereby we will avoid war. That is how the whole debate -- rather than being dedicated to Bosnia-Herzegovina, 59 per cent of it was orientated towards Yugoslavia as a whole. What Serbia's project was regarding the whole of Yugoslavia and what Croatia's project was regarding the whole of Yugoslavia, we were simply intoxicated by this problem and this topic, and a way out of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One remaining little area of interest. In your -- in speaking of your correction, your published partial correction of the Nacional article, it was said there, and I recorded the terms: "This has not substantially distorted what I said." In other words, in your correction you were pointing out certain errors, but you were saying, "Those errors have not substantially distorted what I said." Do you remember that part? And you wrote that correction with your own hand or typewriter. Would that statement also apply to the unpublished part of your correction? Would you be prepared to say, in relation to the unpublished part of your correction --

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In this retraction, I also said that the interpretation regarding the future obstacles to the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not given by President Tudjman, but that I was the one who told them that. But they left that out. They probably had a particular design in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We all know what difficulties reporters can be. So let me ask one last question. If President Tudjman and President Milosevic had an agreement to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you regard that as a matter of substance? Would I then be right in supposing --

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: If you wish to hear my personal opinion then, not today -- not just today but then at the time, I thought that those two leaders wanted to manoeuvre each other and to outwit each other by various proposals and ploys. On one hand to delay the war as far as Croatia was concerned, and as far as Serbia is concerned, to attract Croatia to involve it in a game that would not have been to the benefit of Croatia. That is why I said that our mission of the expert group had mostly to do with Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Politicians, every so often, engage in playing poker games with one another. We know that. You know the expression, "poker game"? Yes. Now, if your first published statement in Nacional referred to an agreement made at Karadjordjevo between the two presidents, then would I be right in supposing that the retraction which you later made was not intended to apply to that matter?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In the part that I was referring to the three obstacles, that did apply, that is that it was not true that I said that to President Tudjman, but I said it to them. Otherwise, I'm afraid I didn't get the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, let me put it back this way then: In your retraction, you said that the errors of which you complained did not distort the substance of the first publication. And my second question was this: If the first publication quoted you or referred to you as referring to Karadjordjevo as establishing an agreement to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you regard that as a matter of substance?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: In my response, a part of which was left out, I said, first of all, that it was to them that I spoke about those three obstacles; and secondly, I said that I never saw any maps, and for some strange reasons, they left that out of my retraction. I tried to write a third retraction, but you see, sometimes the newspaper editors have rather unfair treatment of the author, and they wish to give the impression that they will not change their own positions or their own policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, you encourage me to ask further questions, but it's five minutes to 6.00. You're not so well, and Madam herself is not so well, so I will turn the matter back to the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, indeed. The witness had requested that we be able to finish this evening, so if Judge Riad or Judge Shahabuddeen, if you have any more questions to ask, you may do so. I see. Very well. I understood you to say that you are tired. It has been a very long examination-in-chief and a long cross-examination, but I have a need for some clarification. How long have you been in opposition to Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, I am. As a member of the Central Committee of the Communist party of Croatia, I took part in the continuity of that party which changed its name and became the Social Democratic Party, and which, of course, performed radical changes of its ideology and politics, rejecting the essential traits of Communism. One a uniparty system, second a single-party system, Marxist ideology, the economy, and accepted a multi-party system quite truthfully, adopted market mechanisms and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now I'm going to get to my question. I'm sorry for interrupting you. My question is very simple. You are in opposition. How long have you been in opposition to Mr. Tudjman? That's a very clear, simple question. '88, '89, '90?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: We have been the opposition since the time of the formation. That is when we lost power. We lost power, the Communists, the former Communists, we lost power in May, in the first parliamentary elections of May 1990. And we were forced at the time to join the opposition, and to the present day we have been the opposition, hoping that perhaps at the next elections we will once again take part in the formation of a new ruling power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I understand that is the objective of every opposition is to try to form a new government. If I understand correctly, Mr. Tudjman would call upon you as an advisor. And what kind of functions would you carry out? Are they secrete, are they official or unofficial? He would perhaps ask of you to go on a mission, perhaps to Serbia. What type of role did you play? And I imagine it must not have been a very comfortable one. Do you understand my question? Were you a confidante of President Tudjman, or did he call on for other purposes? I don't quite understand your role.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Thank you. Since 1939, we were the members of the Communist movement. Both of us were Communists, therefore, both of us were partisan for four years. Both of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I understood all of that, but if you want us to let you go very early or very quickly, please try to respond directly to the question.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Then we continued privately from the former regime. We considered to have contacts from time to time. And when we had to go to Belgrade, he started out from the fact that I lived in Belgrade for 20 years, and that I knew many people there, particularly the Belgrade intelligencia, and it was quite normal for him to come to the conclusion that a man of my format, who knows the politicians of Serbia and the intellectuals of Serbia, would be useful to establish contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's a very clear answer. Now, the following question I'd like to ask is about your party. I understand that you are an imminent member of your party. Now, in its own platform, during all these events, did that include a very clear opposition to the issue of Bosnia? Was that one of the central matters in opposition to Tudjman, or did you have other opposition platforms dealing with culture, dealing with the economy, et cetera, or was that a very important platform? And when you met with Mr. Tudjman, because as we've said, you were friends, you said, "My party will not accept that position with regards to that issue." The central point, the pivotal point of the divergence of views between the party and myself lay in the fact that we had a different project with respect to the manner of privatisation of the former socially owned property, with regard to relationships towards the mass media, with respect to the relationship towards state -- legally governed state, based on the very rule of law. And we, who for 50 years tried to realise an ideology, encountered a debacle. We failed. And we considered that we would have to enter a bourgeois society much more decisively, and to develop institutions -- all civil institutions on the multi-party type. And it is the practice of the side that triumphs that once it comes into power, by its very nature, regardless of who the individuals are, it does have the tendency towards authoritarianism. We, however, feel that we have been healed of that disease. I think so. Perhaps we'll be bad too once we come into power, and that is the central question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. We are not here in a political Tribunal, but let me continue with my line of reasoning. So I understand your party was a classical opposition party which had differences with the party in power on various issues. But during the crucial years in 1988 to 1990, given the tragedy that was preparing, in your annual meetings of your party, did it ever issue any strong oppositions, as I have understood, of the maintenance of the internal borders? Is that the case, or did you not deal with that issue?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Communist Party of Croatia was well-known that it was too -- overly-Titoist, and that it was rigid in standing behind the principles of the inviolability of inter-republic borders. And not only that, but we did not, up until the beginning of the downfall of Yugoslavia, we never and even in our imaginations and let alone in reality, did we think that we would agree to a change of borders. We never did that. For us, that was a cannon for the Communists. A dogma, their creed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. So the question I would like to ask now is that during this entire development of a propaganda both in Central Bosnia and perhaps also in Zagreb, and in respect of this possibility for some sort of annex, whether on a cultural basis or historical basis in which this part of Bosnia should become part of Greater Croatia, my question is the following: Did your party do anything? Did it not only state its position but did it also carry out any action? Did it publish any articles? Did it denounce this type of propaganda? Did it state that International Humanitarian Law would be put at risk and all other republics would end up losing... Did your party do anything? And I assume you also heard this propaganda. What is your feeling on that issue? How did your party define itself in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Let me first put right something I said a moment ago. When I said that we were in the opposition from the very first days, I forgot to mention that in the summer of 1991, at the moment of an all-embracing war with the JNA and Serbia, that the so-called government of democratic unity was set up in which the vice-president of my party was the vice-premier of that government of the new regime, and he was there in that post for about one year or a little less, and then in real terms it definitely became what it did. The party never, because we didn't know, at least the public did not know and we did not know, the party never decidedly, at the time when the news came that the meeting was held in Karadjordjevo, it did not decisively say anything, but it always repeated that it stands -- it assumes the positions of the inviolability of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not only that particular party, but this was the stand assumed by the Croatian Popular Party, the Croatia Peasants Party. All of them took that position, all the three or four major parties. The others are not important. They all came out for an unified Bosnia. But you know, when a nation finds itself in war, then the opposition has to retract its horns somewhat. And in order to -- for the purposes of defence, I must state a fact that perhaps you don't know. Never in the history of Croatia did an event occur which occurred in 1990 and 1991, in the war, and that is that three men could not be found who would move towards the side of the aggressor. This fact happened for the first time in the history of Croatia. Croatia, in the Second World War, was tragically divided into two armies which fought for four years, but in this war this did not happen. So as I say, the war and the aggression unified the people to such an extent that the opposition, under such circumstances, did not wish, nor could it sharply criticise the ruling party, because the public would see this as an attack on the newly created state of Croatia, and, therefore, the opposition refrained from doing so. Now it has no such considerations, no such difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that when there are tragic events like this one, the opposition party is obliged to try to nuance its opposition. My following question is the following: Given the traditional basis of your party and the revolutionary history of Communism, during the war against -- when the war against Serbia ended, if it had been proven before you that your country, here we are no longer in the tragic situation of national unity, if it had been proven in one way or another that your country had participated in one way or in another in a plan to infiltrate, or military actions or propaganda into Bosnia, if that had been the case, would you have condemned such an act?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: If it had the power of doing so, it would not have done that, and that emanates from its political strategy, its political doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have fully answered all of the questions. I understand you must be very tired, Professor. I hope that you will be able to catch your plane, and that above all, when you return you will have better news about your wife. Would you like to add something, perhaps? No? Otherwise, it is ended.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Bilandzic.
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Your Honours, I am fully conscious of the vast responsibility that you have taken upon yourselves, because although right and law focuses on man and the individual, you yourselves not only have a man before you, an individual, but you have several nations before you, nations which have gone through this terrible catastrophe. I know full well that you have your consciences and you are aware of the lofty burden that you are bearing, but I have a very happy experience, that is that the Trial Chamber has demonstrated here legal ethics, a Code of Conduct, a legal Code of Conduct which I have found very pleasant, and I must say that I find that your correct attitude is to be commended. If I have helped you in clarifying the situation to you, I am very happy. And as I say, you have a very difficult task you, and as they say, may God help you in your deliberations. Thank you once again. I am happy to have had the opportunity of helping you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, I can tell you already now that you have aided us a great deal, and I can speak on behalf of my colleagues when I say you have our gratitude for having spent two very long days, and we wish you a very serene and agreeable return to your family. Do not leave, do not move as yet. Tomorrow, I believe, Registrar, we are meeting at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, we all stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on the 10th day of September, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
